Case Study — 01

MySensofar.

MySensofar is Sensofar's B2B client platform — used by distributors and customers worldwide to configure, quote and order precision metrology equipment.

Ongoing · Sensofar Tech

2022 – Present

UX Research, Design & Writing

Moderated usability testing

Real product, real users. I designed and ran two moderated usability studies — 4 out of 4 key findings were turned into product improvements and went live in the same release cycle.

My part: I planned and moderated both studies, analysed the findings and designed the proposed changes. Priorities were then agreed with the group in charge of the platform.

The problem
Challenge
"The platform had grown organically, and several friction points had been flagged internally — but never validated with real users."
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
Process
Step 01
Plan
Designed two moderated usability test scripts: one for the Help Center, one for the Sales module (configuration → quotation → approval). Defined realistic scenarios based on actual customer journeys.
2 test scripts Scenario design Task analysis
Step 02
Test
Ran moderated sessions with four internal participants per study, with different levels of platform use and product knowledge. Errors were logged as critical or non-critical.
4 participants per study Scenario cards Error logging
Step 03
Implement
Analysed the sessions and designed the changes myself (labels, interactions and copy), then agreed priorities with the group in charge of the platform. All four improvements shipped within the same release cycle.
UX writing Interaction design 4 shipped

"Users kept clicking 'Summary' expecting to review their selection — not realising it was the button to move forward. Several stopped and asked if they had missed a step."

— Observation, Sales module usability test
4 findings shipped
Finding 01 — Button label caused confusion

The primary action button was labelled "Summary" — users interpreted it as a read-only review, not a call to action. Renamed to "Continue" to communicate forward movement.

Before → After — button label
Finding 02 — Missing navigation context

The breadcrumb only showed the top-level section. Users inside a quotation had no way to know where they were. Adding the subsection level gave users back their location context.

Before — breadcrumb missing
After — location visible
Finding 03 — No feedback after key actions

Users completed key actions with no confirmation or next step. We introduced contextual snackbars — some informative, some with a direct link to the next section.

Contextual snackbars — success & informational
Finding 04 — Legibility issues on white backgrounds

Several UI elements had insufficient contrast on white backgrounds. We iterated on the colour palette to meet accessibility standards.

Contrast iteration — improved legibility
Prioritising what to change

Not every observation became a change. The Help Center study left 13 points to review with the design group and 6 topics for the development team. It found no critical usability errors.

3
To redesign: the favourites icon, the suggested-articles pop-up and fully clickable ticket rows
2
On standby: search plus filtering in the knowledge base, and a smaller banner as part of a general size review
6
Discarded after review, such as moving software products to the first level of the support request
2
Handled another way: a more visible model selector, and a help article on finding the serial number

A deliberate “no”: moving software products to the top level of the support request would have shortened the path, but requests are linked to a product, so the structure stayed.

In the Sales module study, one participant could not finish a task without help because a required choice went unnoticed. That led to the proposal of keeping the buttons always active and showing a message listing the missing required fields.

Outcomes
2
Moderated usability tests designed and run — Help Center and Sales module
4
UX improvements shipped: button label, navigation breadcrumb, snackbars, contrast
4/4
Prioritised findings implemented within the same release cycle
Case Study — 02

Zervice.

A field service management web app for technicians and distributors who install, maintain and repair precision metrology equipment — often in low-connectivity environments.

Master's Thesis (TFM)

2024 – 2025

End-to-end UX Design

Research · Prototyping · Testing

The problem
Challenge
"Technical documentation was scattered across sources and formats, protocols were completed on paper or after the visit, and files sent by hand could get lost or arrive late."
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
Process
Step 01
Discover
Four semi-structured interviews with internal technicians and external distributors, a contextual inquiry on a live recalibration visit, and a benchmark of four field-service platforms.
Semi-structured interviews Contextual inquiry Benchmarking (4 platforms)
Step 02
Define
Four personas, a user journey map and an open card sorting turned the research into a sitemap built around the technician's real task sequence.
Personas User journey map Card sorting Sitemap
Step 03
Design & Test
Wireframes, a high-fidelity interactive prototype in Figma and a moderated in-person usability test with 6 participants.
Figma Usability testing Iteration
Research in practice

Four interviews, one field visit and four competitors — before drawing a single screen.

4Semi-structured interviews: 2 internal technicians, 2 external distributors
1Contextual inquiry on a live recalibration visit
4Platforms benchmarked: Fracttal, GoCanvas, ServiceM8, TrueContext
10Participants in an open card sorting

Research artifacts are shown in their original Spanish. Click any of them to enlarge.

Who I designed for

Four personas built from the interviews and the field observation. Each combines a different role, device habit and pain point.

Mapping one intervention, phase by phase

The journey map follows a technician through six phases — from preparation to final sync — capturing actions, touchpoints, emotions, doubts, pain points and opportunities in each one.

The journey map surfaced the critical moments: the risk of errors when working offline, fatigue from long on-site forms, and uncertainty after sending the final report.

— Key insight from the journey map analysis

That shaped the design: simpler data-entry flows, progress indicators, automatic validation and contextual support.

Letting users decide how content is grouped

An open card sorting — 10 participants, 20 cards, run in UX Tweak — fed a dendrogram that suggested four main categories: Services, Documentation & Resources, Support, and upcoming / past services. I translated them into the app’s information architecture.

The interface

Key screens of the desktop interface, designed for technicians and distributors who manage documentation and service protocols on site. Click any screen to enlarge.

Outcomes
6
Participants in the moderated usability test — all with technical on-site profiles
100%
Of participants completed all main tasks without critical errors
5
Key findings: clear navigation, sound terminology, chat well received, form gaps identified, documentation filters needed
What I’d do differently
01 — Research
More time in the field
I ran four interviews and one contextual inquiry on a live recalibration visit. With more means, I would shadow more technicians on site.
02 — Iteration
Keep testing until it’s final
The usability test with 6 participants validated the design. With more means, I would keep running test rounds and iterating until reaching a final design.
03 — Scope
More sections and flows
The design covers the core installation flow. Maintenance and repair need their own flows, and the offline mode needs clearer sync and pending-send states.

As a proof of concept, an MVP, I think it worked well.

Case Study — 03

Mantfer.

Mantfer is a local plumbing, drain-clearing and maintenance business in Ripollet and Barcelona. With over 20 years in the trade but no online presence, they were entirely dependent on word of mouth. I designed their first website end to end, adapting the copy across three languages.

Freelance client

2026

UX Design & Copy optimisation

Catalan · Spanish · English

The problem
Challenge
"20+ years of trade experience, zero online presence. Every new customer came from word of mouth — with no way to reach the people searching for this exact service in their area."
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
Process
Step 01
Research
Analysed local competitors and how people actually search for this type of service — urgent, local, trust-driven decisions, often made on mobile in the moment. Ran a card sorting exercise with a sample of prospective users to validate how services should be grouped.
Competitor analysis Local SEO research Card sorting
Step 02
Structure & copy
Defined the information architecture and optimised the copy across three languages for clarity and conversion — prioritising fast trust signals and a low-friction path to contact.
IA Conversion copy CA / ES / EN
Step 03
Design
Designed a mobile-first site built around urgency and trust — persistent call-to-action, clear service breakdown, and a guided multi-step quote request.
Mobile-first Design system
Step 04
Validate
Tested the design with real prospective users first, then refined it further with the client before launch.
User testing Client review
